summary:
Castilla y León stands under Spain's national framework. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of the acquired gender is possible from age 12 under conditions.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in the region.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months. Both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts apply the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005.

Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community never to have enacted a regional LGTBI or gender-identity law. For a trans visitor the vacuum is administrative rather than punitive. No criminal ban and no facility restriction exists in the region, national criminal law applies in full, and the severity floor is therefore set by the state. What the region lacks is dedicated machinery: no regional equality office receives complaints, no institutional hate-crime observatory operates, and no region-specific administrative protocol governs responses to gender-motivated incidents.

Legislative movement is under way. The PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León on 20 December 2024, explicitly aimed at ending the "sexilio", the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, and group leader Tudanca urged the fastest possible processing. On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the bill into consideration; it runs to 76 articles and answers long-standing demands of regional LGBTI+ collectives. The PP abstained, Vox voted against, and LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.
tangentialFactors:
The pending regional bill is framed by its sponsors as a response to "sexilio", the out-migration of LGBTI people from Castilla y León, a term the PSOE group used when registering the legislation in December 2024.

Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries, and with administrative self-declaration it stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

The vote of 11 June 2025 turned on abstention rather than majority support: the PP's abstention allowed the bill to be taken into consideration while Vox opposed it. Regional press reported that LGBTI advocates expect the committee stage to be where the process stalls.
localsOnly:
Residents of Castilla y León rectify the gender mention on their registry entry through the Civil Registry under national law, with no regional procedure, no regional authorisation, no diagnosis and no period of treatment.

Because the region operates no equality office and no hate-crime observatory, a resident reporting a gender-motivated incident has no regional body to approach; the complaint machinery available is the national one.

Residents aged 12 to 16 hold consent rights over medical procedures under Ley 4/2023, and recognition of the acquired gender from age 12 is possible under conditions, all of which apply here despite the absence of a regional statute.

Residents are the stated constituency of the bill tabled in December 2024, whose sponsors argue that the lack of regional legislation has driven LGBTI people to leave the region.
